lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why freedom comes whole
lead.head: Freedom isn’t sold separately
body: “Can we grow rich and still beat our wives? Or do we have to stop beating our wives to grow rich?” The question came from a friend of Amit Varma’s who runs one of Asia’s biggest businesses, and who let Varma use the question but not his name. {016-S01}

At heart, Varma said, it asks whether prosperity needs modernity: freedom, consent, autonomy. His answer is that all kinds of freedom have to come hand in hand, and that true prosperity, even in the material sense, is impossible without them. {016-C01}
When Varma first told him the question, Ajay Shah said at once that it belonged in their episode on China. What followed was a history of two great bets against freedom.
## The Soviet bet
The Soviet Union bet that freedom mattered in no domain. It forced industrialisation through central planning and cruelty, built a nuclear bomb by 1949, and looked to many like the future.
Then, in 1989, it collapsed under the weight of its own contradictions.
Shah borrowed a term from computer engineering: technical debt. “You can appear to make some progress, but your sins are going to catch up with you,” he said. {016-C02}
Behind it all were ideas. “Nothing matters more than ideas,” Shah said, and in every free country a camp of thinkers has argued for less freedom. They admired the Soviet Union first, and China next.
## The China bet

The Chinese Communist Party studied the Soviet fall and drew a lesson: shortages kill regimes. So it opened up to consumer goods, trade and foreign investment, while keeping one-party rule and limits on personal freedom.
For a while it worked. Hundreds of millions of people came out of poverty, and global firms committed themselves to the China story.

Now, Shah argued, the model is breaking. He named five forces: Xi Jinping’s return to Maoist and Leninist politics, the mismanagement of COVID, confrontation with the advanced economies, unsustainable economic management and a populist attack on the country’s other elites.
“This whole package of grievance and anger and nationalism is really toxic and the China model is broken and it will not work,” he said. {016-C20}
The regime is in charge and the border is intact. But like the Soviet model in 1989, he said, the China model has lost its credibility.
## Ends and means
Amit Varma retold the story from Mao onwards, through Adam Smith’s “man of system”, the planner in love with his own plan, and through the Leninist machinery that still runs beneath China’s reforms.

He also pressed the other side. Deng Xiaoping’s China gave a generation the kind of mobility that India, Varma said, still does not see. If Deng’s aim was to lift a few hundred million people out of poverty, he argued, he succeeded.
Shah replied that great statesmen play for 50 and 100 years, and on that measure Taiwan, not China, has got its act together.
“You need to really fix the freedom side first. You need to get on the journey to a lot more freedom. Then good things will come,” he said. {016-C19}
He even had a book in mind for Deng: *In Service of the Republic*, which he wrote with Vijay Kelkar. Varma called it the greatest plug he had ever seen anyone give their own book.
On the larger point, there was no quarrel. “Freedom is everything,” Varma said.

second.label: The Great Leap Forward
second.head: The sparrow’s revenge
second.deck: Amit Varma on Mao’s 1958 campaign and the delusion of the master plan
body: In 1958, Mao ordered every sparrow in China killed. Farmers were suffering because sparrows ate their grain, and the campaign was hailed as a necessary step by a strong leader. {016-S06}

Countless sparrows died. But sparrows ate locusts, and once they were gone, locusts multiplied and destroyed China’s crops. No fewer than 45 million people died in the three years that followed. {#famine}

Amit Varma read the passage aloud before revealing its author: himself, in a 2016 column on demonetisation. The sparrow campaign, he had written, was one of many edicts of the Great Leap Forward, all born of the delusion that a leader could redesign a whole society to fit a master plan.

quote.text: Sparrows ate locusts. And once the balance in the ecosystem changed, locusts proliferated and destroyed China’s crops.

second.caption: Mao’s war on sparrows

third.head: Let them eat yogurt
body: When the Soviet Union fell, the Chinese Communist Party studied it intensively, Ajay Shah said, and swore to do whatever it took to survive.
It drew a homely lesson. “They understood that the Soviet Union collapsed because they were not able to make more than four kinds of flavoured yogurt,” Shah said. {016-S03}

So China opened up to a private consumer economy with 400 kinds of yogurt, to trade and to foreign investment. The state stayed on top, with one-party rule and limits on personal freedom. “And by God,” Shah said, “they did ignite a growth process.”

It also showed what coercion can coordinate. China did much the same as India’s UPI, forcing everyone onto one payment standard, and quick, visible wins like that persuaded admirers that wise officials could guide an economy. {016-C03}
third.caption: four flavours of yogurt

p2.title: The broken model
p2.deck: Moscow bet freedom was unnecessary, Beijing that a little would do. Amit Varma says it comes as a package. {016-C01}

sections.label: The question
sections.head: The tycoon’s dinner question
sections.caption: a question of wives and wealth
body: Over dinner abroad, a friend of Amit Varma’s asked a question so beautifully formed that Varma asked if he could quote him. The friend, who runs one of the biggest businesses in Asia and holds degrees in philosophy and anthropology, said no to his name but yes to the question. {016-S01}

Can we grow rich and still beat our wives, or must we stop to grow rich? At heart, Varma said, it is a question about modernity, by which he means classical liberal values: freedom, consent and autonomy.

The median Indian male, he guessed, would answer that prosperity and tradition can come together. Varma’s own position, which he called controversial, is that true prosperity in all its senses, even the material sense, is impossible in the long run without modernity. {016-C01}
## Two lenses
Ajay Shah suggested two ways into the question. The first is to ask whether the answer differs for an individual, who may get ahead with Neanderthal values, and for a whole society.

The second is to suppose the answer is no: that prosperity needs “the full package of enlightenment values”, and the package is not divisible. Some would then make their peace with those values. Others, Shah wondered, might choose to sacrifice the prosperity. {#sacrifice}
~ Shah had said, when Varma first put the question to him, that it belonged in their China episode. The China story, Varma said, is not really about China. “It’s about all of us.”

quote.text: If we are to prosper as people, to grow as individuals, all kinds of freedom have to come hand in hand.

sections.label: The first bet
sections.head: Moscow’s sprint, Moscow’s debt
sections.caption: the Soviet backdrop
body: The Soviet Union, Amit Varma said, rested on the claim that freedom mattered in no domain, personal, economic or political. That was a lie twice over: the prosperity was a lie, and a system like that had to give.

Varma explained the fall with Timur Kuran’s idea of preference falsification. Under repression, every individual was scared to speak up, so nobody seemed to be against the regime. Once people saw that others felt the same, the silence became a preference cascade. {016-C06}
Ajay Shah called the regime’s early growth a sprint that ran up technical debt, a phrase from computer engineering. {016-C02}
## A camp that never leaves

The Soviet Union’s disasters and achievements alike, Shah said, were the work of “an academic scribbler called Karl Marx”, who never saw the outside world beyond the British Library. {016-J11} In every free country, he added, a camp of thinkers has argued for less freedom. {016-C04}

Some argued that a poor country should be thuggish first and add democracy later. It was a great debate of the Indian freedom movement, Shah said, when female literacy in 1947 was 6 or 7 per cent. {#literacy}
~ Chile, Taiwan and South Korea made the move from dictatorship, he said, but it is not easy. The Soviet economy was so distorted that 1989 burned it to the ground.

quote.text: So in the end, it is all about ideas. Nothing matters more than ideas.

sections.label: The second bet
sections.head: Right way, wrong turn
sections.caption: the China model and COVID
body: For a while, Ajay Shah said, the China model seemed to work. Hundreds of millions came out of poverty, and global capitalism, whose practitioners “go along with a prevailing consensus”, committed itself to the China story.

Amit Varma recalled a scene from Richard McGregor’s *The Party*. In 2008, with the financial crisis just breaking in America, Wang Qishan, the vice premier in charge of finance, told visiting American businessmen: “You have your way. We have our way, our way is right.” {016-S04}
Then came Xi Jinping, and with him, Shah said, “a huge step back towards Maoism”.
## The vaccine nobody trusted

COVID exposed the cost. India made no pretence of building its own vaccine, Shah said: the Oxford-AstraZeneca shot came with help from the Gates Foundation and was made at giant scale by a private Indian company. China, insisting it had arrived, pushed its own vaccines, which protected poorly. {016-S10}
Many older Chinese refused them. “So if the government says this is a made in China vaccine, you know something is wrong,” Shah said. Plenty, he added, will not even drink made-in-China milk.

~ Varma added that the distrust is practical, not moral: authoritarian governments face bad incentives and “will always be incompetent”. {016-C14} Each act of cruelty, Shah replied, teaches a hundred friends and family that the regime cannot be trusted. {#bayes}

quote.text: When you’ve lived in an authoritarian country, you know the government is an enemy and not a friend.

sections.label: The perfect storm
sections.head: Target practice
sections.caption: the perfect storm
body: Ajay Shah flagged an uncomfortable phrase used in China, one he said no free country should use: macroeconomic management.

Officials pulled four levers, land, construction, infrastructure and credit, to hit a GDP target year after year, and on paper China had conquered the business cycle. “So whenever there’s a GDP target, you gotta get nervous that something is not going right in this country,” Shah said. {016-C10}
Infrastructure built to prop up growth could be a road to nowhere. A private developer would not build one, Shah said, because it worries about getting paid. {016-C11}

Amit Varma, who objects that GDP counts government spending, said of such growth: “it is a shadow, it is a chimera”. He added that their own show was a road to nowhere: “It’s a labour of love, no returns.”
## Never a bad year

Capitalism needs booms and busts to create the right incentives, Shah argued. {016-C12} China’s pump-priming produced 50-year-old business leaders who had never known a downturn, and capital went to whoever borrowed most and cosied up to the party.
Then Xi Jinping turned the state on the other three elites, business, intellectual and cultural, and families sent their children and money abroad. {016-C13}
~ Nor was it wise to pick fights with the advanced economies, Shah said, which make up 60 to 70 per cent of world GDP. {#worldgdp}

quote.text: A good infrastructure project is one that earns some plausible return on equity.

sections.label: Through the decades
sections.head: Pawns with minds of their own
sections.caption: the man of system
body: Amit Varma began his history of modern China with Mao, and with Adam Smith’s “man of system”, who imagines he can arrange a society like pieces on a chessboard. Friedrich Hayek called the same error the fatal conceit. {016-C07}

Deng Xiaoping changed much, but not the machine. Reading from Richard McGregor’s *The Party*, Varma said the party kept its grip on personnel, propaganda and the army. One university professor, quoted by McGregor, put it this way: “The party is like God. He is everywhere. You just can’t see him.” {016-J14}
In place of terror came what McGregor calls a take-it-or-leave-it compact: stay out of politics, and you and your family can get on with your lives and maybe get rich. {016-C09}
## Two cars
Many did. In *Smoke and Mirrors*, Pallavi Aiyar recorded a student whose father had cycled miles to work and who now owned two cars. Everybody, she told Varma, said some version of it. {016-S08}
Did that end justify the means? Not for Ajay Shah: state murder and cruelty are beyond the pale, and gains in income add less to happiness than people assume. {016-C17}
~ Nor, he argued, does coercive growth last. Authoritarian rule breeds a culture of obedience that kills initiative and creativity, and the knowledge of how to be free cannot be switched on at will.

quote.text: In the great chessboard of human society, every single piece has a principle of motion of its own
quote.who: Adam Smith, as read by Amit Varma

side.boxText: Deng Xiaoping built term limits, a succession system and a stance of biding time with the West. Xi Jinping, Ajay Shah said, undid them, concentrated power in himself and his cronies, and fanned nationalism among young men. {#termlimits}

contQuote.text: As long as there is a certain level of elite capability, it can be the bridge and connect into globalisation. And then you’re off to the races.

stories.start: In 1905, Tsarist Russia lost a war to Japan.
stories.end: you had to wake up in 1989 and say that, look, this didn't work
stories.caption: Samuelson’s dotted line
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on when the USSR looked like the future
stories.head: Samuelson’s dots never joined
body: The most important economics textbook in world history, Ajay Shah said, carried a prophecy on its inside cover. In edition after edition, Paul Samuelson printed there a chart of the GDP of various countries.
“Samuelson always had a dot dot dot line with projections for the future where he expected that the USSR would beat the United States in terms of its aggregate GDP,” Shah said. {016-S02}

The faith had a history. In 1905 Tsarist Russia lost a war to Japan. After the revolution of 1917 came forced modernisation: factories, science, technology and five-year plans, along with what Shah called “mind-boggling levels of cruelty”. Millions were murdered.

By 1945 the Soviet Union had beaten Adolf Hitler, with a great deal of Western help, and was the great land power of the world. By 1949 it had a nuclear bomb, built partly on ideas stolen from the Manhattan Project. {#bomb}
George Orwell, Arthur Koestler and Jawaharlal Nehru all rejected the regime’s cruelty. But many still believed that, in a purely instrumental way, the model was going to work.

It did not. The projection, Shah said, never came true. In 1989 the Soviet Union collapsed under the weight of its own contradictions, and the occupied lands, festering with hatred and resentment, walked away the moment they could.
~ Russia, Shah said, has never got its mojo back. “It’s a Spain sized GDP. Frankly, it’s just Saudi Arabia with nukes.” {016-J01}
stories.why: Even the best economists can mistake a coercive sprint for a durable growth model. The case for unfreedom, Shah argued, failed on its own instrumental terms, not only on ethical ones.
stories.postscript: When Shah likened Russia to Spain and Saudi Arabia, Amit Varma imagined listeners from both countries protesting, in Hindi, at being dragged in.

stories.start: So when Mao Zedong pulled off that giant trauma, which was the Cultural Revolution
stories.end: it's a Deng Xiaoping phrase that don't don't pick fights on these things
stories.caption: Deng Xiaoping’s son
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the cruelty that shaped China’s reformer
stories.head: A son, a window, and term limits
body: During the Cultural Revolution, Ajay Shah said, Red Guards threw Deng Xiaoping’s son, then about 11 or 14 years old, out of a first-floor window. The boy broke his bones and was crippled for life. {016-S05}
“So, in a way, Deng Xiaoping deeply knew the horror of Chinese communism,” Shah said. When Deng came to power in 1978, he had no illusions about the regime.

He built guardrails. The head of state could serve only ten years, and a succession system was created where Mao and the Soviet Union had none. Abroad, Deng’s phrase was “we should bide our time”: China was weak, needed Western technology and capital, and should not pick fights. {016-J12}
~ Xi Jinping, Shah said, undid it all. He abandoned the term limits and gathered power to himself and his cronies. {#termlimits}
stories.why: The reforms came from a man who had felt the regime’s cruelty in his own family. That explains why he spread power out, and why Xi gathering it back matters so much.

stories.start: China came up with the world's most extreme lockdowns
stories.end: there was a great surge of COVID, and lots of people died
stories.caption: China’s lockdowns
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on China’s lockdowns and the phone as jailer
stories.head: One street too far
body: China met COVID with some of the world’s most extreme lockdowns, Ajay Shah said, and with a triumphalism that the Chinese way was better. Month after month, people were trapped in their homes.

Mobile phones, digital identity and tracking were turned against them. “People could not move into the next street because the app would start screaming, and then a government official would come after that person,” Shah said. {016-S11}
Factories stopped, flights stopped, and supply chains around the world were disrupted. There were even protests on the streets, which Shah called very unusual in China.
~ Far from a triumph, Shah said, China became the world’s worst COVID nightmare. In the end the regime gave up. COVID surged, and lots of people died. {#surge}

quote.text: the ability of the modern digital revolution to destroy the lives of individuals when placed in the hands of an authoritarian country

stories.start: this is a passage that when I read it in Smoke and Mirrors
stories.end: beyond the point, you begin to wonder that how long can that culture remain
stories.caption: songbirds and bulldozers
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s lament for cultures under long tyranny
stories.head: Songbirds on the expressway
body: In Pallavi Aiyar’s *Smoke and Mirrors*, Beijing is a surreal place. Old bent men in Mao suits walk their caged songbirds along an expressway. {#songbirds} Elderly women practise tai chi surrounded by bulldozers.

What struck Aiyar most was “the lack of visible trauma or resistance”. Amit Varma found that sad and worrying. Part of him believes bottom-up culture always outlasts top-down rule; another part says cultural change can be driven by state coercion, especially the longer a regime lasts: as they say, paradigms change one funeral at a time.
Sometimes, he said, the oppressive regime may win. {016-S09}

~ He saw that tension in Lahore in 2006, following the Indian cricket team as a journalist. His father was born there but felt no nostalgia for it. Varma found a warm, effusive Punjabi culture, and beside it a darkness coming from the regime’s ideology.

quote.text: Sometimes in this clash between an oppressive regime and a liberated culture, the oppressive regime may win out.
